# SQLite: WAL vs rollback journal for concurrent writes

*Generated by Quoteproof: 78 claims from 5 angles, 71 kept after cross-examination and quote checking.*

## Key findings

1. **Neither mode allows concurrent writers.** SQLite permits many readers but "only one simultaneous write transaction" ([lang_transaction](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html)). In WAL, "there can only be one writer at a time" ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). What WAL changes is *reader/writer* concurrency.
2. **WAL removes reader↔writer blocking.** "Readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers" ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). In rollback mode a PENDING writer blocks new readers, and once the page cache spills, "no other processes are able to access the database" until commit ([lockingv3](https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html)).
3. **WAL writes are cheaper.** Content is written once instead of twice ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)), with "many fewer fsync() operations" ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). With `synchronous=NORMAL`, "no sync operations occur during most transactions" ([pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)); the checkpoint is the only sync barrier ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)).
4. **The speed comes from trading durability.** WAL+NORMAL "is always consistent … but does lose durability": a committed transaction "might roll back following a power loss" ([pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)). WAL+FULL is fully ACID, syncing the WAL on every commit ([pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html), [wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). All modes are durable across *application* crashes ([pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)).
5. **Rollback+FULL is weaker than it sounds.** "FULL is not necessarily durable across a power loss in rollback mode"; `EXTRA` adds a directory sync to close that gap. EXTRA is identical to FULL in WAL ([pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)).

## Recommendations

| Situation | Choose | Why |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Local disk, mixed read/write, can lose last commit on power loss | **WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL`** | Docs: "best balance between performance and safety for most applications running in WAL mode" ([pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)) |
| Every acknowledged commit must survive power loss | **WAL + `synchronous=FULL`** | ACID in WAL; still no reader/writer blocking |
| Database on a network filesystem | **Rollback journal** (and reconsider SQLite) | WAL "does not work over a network filesystem" ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)); locking over NFS has caused corruption ([useovernet](https://www.sqlite.org/useovernet.html)) |
| One transaction must span several ATTACHed DBs atomically | **Rollback journal** | WAL is atomic per DB only; rollback uses a super-journal for cross-file atomicity ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html), [atomiccommit](https://sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html)) |
| Shipping DB on read-only media | **`journal_mode=DELETE`** before burning | Docs' stated good practice ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)) |

```sql
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;        -- persistent: sticks to the file
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;      -- or FULL if power-loss durability matters
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;       -- per connection; otherwise lock conflicts fail immediately
-- writers: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so a write lock conflict surfaces at BEGIN, not mid-transaction
```

`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` matters because a `DEFERRED` transaction that later tries to write "will fail with SQLITE_BUSY" if another connection has modified the DB meanwhile — and the busy timeout can't help there ([lang_transaction](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html)).

## Trade-offs and failure modes in WAL

- **Checkpoint starvation.** If there is always at least one active reader, "no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound" ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). Read speed degrades as the WAL grows, since every reader must consult it ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). Fix: leave reader gaps, or run `RESTART`/`TRUNCATE` checkpoints, which may block readers while running ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)).
- **Commit latency spikes.** Auto-checkpoint (PASSIVE, at 1000 pages) runs inside the COMMIT that crosses the threshold, so "an occasional COMMIT … [is] much slower" ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)). Move checkpoints to a background thread with `wal_autocheckpoint=0` if this matters.
- **WAL file never shrinks by default.** Checkpoints rewind but don't truncate unless `journal_size_limit` is set; default is no limit ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html), [pragma](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)).
- **Shared memory required.** The `-shm` file is mmapped next to the DB; opening needs write access to it or its directory, and a VFS without shm support can't use WAL at all — unless `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE` is set first ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)).
- **Read-heavy apps** may run ~1–2% slower in WAL ([wal](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)).

## Measured numbers (low confidence)

One secondary benchmark (10,000 autocommitted inserts) reports ~279 inserts/s for DELETE+FULL, ~442/s for WAL+FULL, ~33,135/s for WAL+NORMAL ([sesamedisk](https://sesamedisk.com/sqlite-performance-tuning-high-throughput/)). Single unreplicated source — directionally consistent with the fsync analysis above (the jump is from dropping per-commit sync, not from WAL alone), but measure on your own hardware.

## Open questions

- **True concurrent writers** exist only on unmerged branches: `BEGIN CONCURRENT` (optimistic page-level concurrency in wal/wal2) and `wal2` (two WAL files, avoids starvation) ([begin-concurrent](https://sqlite.org/cgi/src/doc/begin-concurrent/doc/begin_concurrent.md), [wal2](https://sqlite.org/cgi/src/doc/wal2/doc/wal2.md)). Not in mainline SQLite; status unverified.
- **Dropped in verification:** "rollback is faster for transactions >100 MB" and "WAL may fail for >1 GB transactions" — wal.html follows them with "Beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), WAL mode works as efficiently with large transactions as does rollback mode," so they describe pre-2016 behaviour.
